usamo-usamo-1989-02.title: Maximum matching
usamo-usamo-1989-02.body:
Make a graph: members are vertices, games are edges; there are $20$ vertices, $14$ edges and no isolated vertex. A set of games with distinct players is a *matching*.

Take a matching $E$ with the largest possible number $k$ of edges, and suppose $k \le 5$. Its edges cover $2k$ vertices; the other $20 - 2k \ge 10$ vertices form a set $W$.

- No edge joins two vertices of $W$ (it could be added to $E$, contradicting maximality).
- Each vertex of $W$ lies on some edge, which therefore joins it to a covered vertex. These edges are different for different vertices of $W$ (each has only one endpoint in $W$), and none of them is in $E$.

So the graph has at least $k + (20 - 2k) = 20 - k \ge 15$ edges, contradicting $14$. Hence $k \ge 6$: some 6 games involve 12 distinct players. ∎

usamo-usamo-1989-02.title: Minimal covering set of games
usamo-usamo-1989-02.body:
Choose a set $F$ of games that still includes every member, with $|F|$ as small as possible (the whole schedule is such a set, so $|F| \le 14$).

$F$ contains no path of three games $x\!-\!y\!-\!z\!-\!w$ (the middle game $yz$ could be removed: $y$ and $z$ still play other games in $F$) and no cycle (removing any game of a cycle keeps everyone covered). So each connected component of $F$ is a tree without a path of length 3, i.e. a *star* (one centre joined to some leaves).

A star with $j$ edges has $j+1$ vertices, so if $F$ has $s$ components, $20 = |F| + s \le 14 + s$, giving $s \ge 6$. Pick one game from each of six different stars: these six games have $12$ distinct players. ∎

usamo-usamo-1989-03.title: Pair conjugate roots
usamo-usamo-1989-03.body:
Since $|P(i)| < 1 \ne |1|$, $P$ is not the constant $1$, so $n \ge 1$. Write $P(z) = \prod_{j=1}^n (z - z_j)$. Because the coefficients are real, non-real roots come in conjugate pairs $w, \overline w$ of equal multiplicity. Split the roots into real roots $r$ and pairs $\{w, \overline{w}\}$. Then
$$1 > |P(i)| = \prod_{\text{real } r}|i - r| \cdot \prod_{\text{pairs}}|i - w|\,|i - \overline w|.$$
For a real root, $|i - r| = \sqrt{r^2 + 1} \ge 1$. So the product over pairs is less than $1$ (in particular there is at least one pair), and some pair $w = a + bi$, $\overline w = a - bi$ has $|i - w|\,|i - \overline w| < 1$.

Now
$$|i - w|^2\,|i - \overline w|^2 = \left(a^2 + (b-1)^2\right)\left(a^2 + (b+1)^2\right) = (a^2 + b^2 + 1 - 2b)(a^2+b^2+1+2b) = (a^2 + b^2 + 1)^2 - 4b^2.$$
Hence $(a^2 + b^2 + 1)^2 - 4b^2 < 1$, i.e. $(a^2+b^2+1)^2 < 4b^2 + 1$, and $P(a + bi) = P(w) = 0$. ∎

usamo-usamo-1989-04.title: Locate $I$ among the six small triangles
usamo-usamo-1989-04.body:
Let the angles be $A, B, C$. From $AB < AC < BC$ we get $C < B < A$. The triangle is acute, so $O$ is inside it; let $D, E, F$ be the points where lines $AO, BO, CO$ meet $BC, CA, AB$. The cevians $AD, BE, CF$ cut $ABC$ into six triangles around $O$.

**Angles at the vertices.** Triangle $AOB$ is isosceles with $\angle AOB = 2C$, so $\angle OAB = \angle OBA = 90^\circ - C$. Likewise $\angle OBC = \angle OCB = 90^\circ - A$ and $\angle OCA = \angle OAC = 90^\circ - B$. The bisector from each vertex makes half the vertex angle with each side.

- **At $A$:** $\angle BAO = 90^\circ - C$ and $\angle CAO = 90^\circ - B$, with $90^\circ - C > 90^\circ - B$. So $\angle BAO > \frac A2$: ray $AI$ lies strictly between $AB$ and $AO$, i.e. $I$ is strictly on $B$'s side of line $AD$.
- **At $B$:** $\angle CBO = 90^\circ - A < 90^\circ - C = \angle ABO$, so $\angle CBO < \frac B2$: ray $BI$ lies strictly between $BO$ and $BA$, i.e. $I$ is strictly on $A$'s side of line $BE$.
- **At $C$:** $\angle BCO = 90^\circ - A < 90^\circ - B = \angle ACO$, so $\angle BCO < \frac C2$: ray $CI$ lies strictly between $CO$ and $CA$, i.e. $I$ is strictly on $A$'s side of line $CF$.

The six small triangles on $B$'s side of $AD$ are $AOF, FOB, BOD$; on $A$'s side of $BE$ they are $EOA, AOF, FOB$; on $A$'s side of $CF$ they are $COE, EOA, AOF$. The only common one is $AOF$, so **$I$ lies inside triangle $AOF$** (and $I \ne O$).

**Conclusion.** The ray from vertex $O$ through the interior point $I$ of triangle $AOF$ leaves it through the opposite side $AF$, a part of segment $AB$. The opposite ray from $O$ lies inside the vertical angle of $\angle AOF$, which is $\angle DOC$ (since $A, O, D$ and $F, O, C$ are collinear), so it meets segment $DC$, a part of $BC$. Hence line $IO$ meets segments $AB$ and $BC$. ∎

usamo-usamo-1989-05.title: Compare the two functions on $(0, 0.9)$
usamo-usamo-1989-05.body:
Let $U(x) = x + x^2 + \cdots + x^8 + 10x^9$ and $V(x) = x + x^2 + \cdots + x^{10} + 10x^{11}$, so $U(u) = V(v) = 8$. Both are strictly increasing on $[0, \infty)$ (all coefficients positive).

**Both roots are in $(0, 0.9)$.**
- For $x \le 0$: $x + \cdots + x^9 = \frac{x^{10} - x}{x - 1} \le 0$ (numerator $\ge 0$, denominator $< 0$), and $U(x) = (x + \cdots + x^9) + 9x^9 \le 0 < 8$. Similarly $V(x) = \frac{x^{12}-x}{x-1} + 9x^{11} \le 0$.
- At $x = 0.9$: $U(0.9) = \frac{0.9(1 - 0.9^9)}{0.1} + 9\cdot 0.9^9 = 9$, and similarly $V(0.9) = 9(1 - 0.9^{11}) + 9\cdot 0.9^{11} = 9$. As $U, V$ increase on $[0,\infty)$, both exceed $8$ for $x \ge 0.9$.

So $u, v \in (0, 0.9)$.

**Comparison.** For $x \in (0, 0.9)$,
$$V(x) - U(x) = x^{9} + x^{10} + 10x^{11} - 10x^9 = x^9(10x^2 + x - 9) = x^9(10x - 9)(x+1) < 0.$$
Hence $V(u) < U(u) = 8 = V(v)$, and since $V$ is increasing on $[0, \infty)$, $u < v$.

**Answer: $v$ is larger.** ∎
